        "pd.read_sql_query(\n",
        "    \"\"\"select education, COUNT(*) AS total_contacted,\n",
        "       SUM(CASE WHEN deposit = 'yes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS subscribed,\n",
        "       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN deposit = 'yes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)\n",
        "             / COUNT(*), 2) AS subscription_rate_pct\n",
        "       FROM bank\n",
        "      GROUP BY education\n",
        "      ORDER BY subscribed DESC;\"\"\", conn)"

        "##Part 2. Feature Engineering and Encoding (20%)"
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "AKyatrJ1Yb4G"
      }
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "source": [
        "The features engineering will be age group"
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "5rpVq73PYiyE"
      }
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "source": [
        "Feature 1 — age_group: Binning Age into Life Stages\n",
        "Business reasoning: A 22-year-old and a 60-year-old face very different financial realities. Binning age into life stages (Youth, Young Adults, Middle-Aged Adults, Older Adults, Elderly) lets the model capture non-linear relationships between age and deposit behaviour. For example, older adults approaching retirement may be more receptive to term deposits as a safe savings vehicle, while youth may prefer liquidity. A raw integer age column cannot easily express this without the model seeing enough data at each age point."
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "ShazHrES0zry"
      }
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "code",
      "source": [
        "#creating bins for age\n",
        "bins=[0,25,35,50,65,100]\n",
        "labels = [\n",
        "    \"Youth\",\n",
        "    \"Young Adults\",\n",
        "    \"Middle-Aged Adults\",\n",
        "    \"Older Adults\",\n",
        "    \"Elderly\"\n",
        "]\n",
        "\n",
        "df['age_group']=pd.cut(df['age'],bins=bins, labels=labels)\n",
        "\n",
        "df.head()"
      ],

    {
      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "source": [
        "### Feature 2 — `pdays_clean`, `pdays_clean1`, `pdays_group`: Contact Recency Features\n",
        "\n",
        "**Business reasoning:** `pdays` is -1 for customers never previously contacted, which is a sentinel value, not a real number. We clean this in three steps:\n",
        "- Replace -1 with 999 (`pdays_clean`) so it sorts naturally as 'long ago or never.'\n",
        "- Create a binary flag `pdays_clean1` (1 = was contacted before, 0 = never) to isolate the yes/no signal.\n",
        "- Bin `pdays_clean` into recency buckets (`pdays_group`: Recent, 1-3 Months, etc.) because the difference between being contacted 5 days ago vs 25 days ago matters more than the difference between 200 vs 250 days ago. Binning compresses the long right tail into meaningful business intervals.\n",
        "\n",
        "### Feature 3 — `has_previous_contact1`: Prior Campaign Engagement Flag\n",
        "\n",
        "**Business reasoning:** The `previous` column counts how many times a customer was contacted before this campaign. A customer with any prior contact has already shown willingness to engage with the bank, which is a positive signal. We convert this to a binary flag because the marginal difference between 3 and 4 prior contacts is small, but the difference between 0 and 1 is large.\n",
        "\n",
        "### Feature 4 — `high_balance`: Above-Median Account Balance Flag\n",
        "\n",
        "**Business reasoning:** Customers with higher account balances are more likely to have surplus savings to lock into a term deposit. We create a simple binary flag splitting customers above and below the median balance. This is more robust than using raw balance, which is heavily skewed by outliers."
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "C20Ue3FBcKuI"
      }
    },

        "### Analysis: Combined Effect of Contact History and Balance on Subscription\n",
        "\n",
        "This analysis groups customers by three features:\n",
        "- `pdays_clean1` (previous contact indicator)\n",
        "- `has_previous_contact1` (contact history)\n",
        "- `high_balance` (financial strength)\n",
        "\n",
        "and examines their subscription outcome (`deposit`).\n",
        "\n",
        "#### Key Observations:\n",
        "\n",
        "- **No previous contact & low balance (0, 0, 0):**\n",
        "  - 2,807 did not subscribe\n",
        "  - 1,539 subscribed  \n",
        "  → Low conversion rate\n",
        "\n",
        "- **No previous contact & high balance (0, 0, 1):**\n",
        "  - 2,133 did not subscribe\n",
        "  - 1,845 subscribed  \n",
        "  → Slightly better conversion than low balance\n",
        "\n",
        "- **Previous contact & low balance (1, 1, 0):**\n",
        "  - 755 subscribed\n",
        "  - 482 did not subscribe  \n",
        "  → Higher conversion rate\n",
        "\n",
        "- **Previous contact & high balance (1, 1, 1):**\n",
        "  - 1,150 subscribed\n",
        "  - 451 did not subscribe  \n",
        "  → Highest conversion rate\n",
        "\n",
        "#### Interpretation:\n",
        "\n",
        "- Previous contact significantly increases the likelihood of subscription\n",
        "- High balance further improves conversion within each group\n",
        "- The combination of **previous contact + high balance** produces the best results"

      "cell_type": "markdown",

        "K-Means Clustering K-Means groups customers based on their feature values, without knowing anything about their churn label. First we decide how many groups (K) to ask for."
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "irOn9oTZvCme"
      }
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "source": [
        "The Elbow Method We fit K-Means at different values of K and record inertia, which measures how tight the clusters are."
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "ixp2w9SnvD5M"
      }
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "source": [
        "\"We run K-Means with K from 2 to 10 to find the optimal number of clusters. The elbow curve shows where adding more clusters stops improving the model significantly. Silhouette score measures how well each customer fits into its assigned cluster — closer to 1 is better.\""
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "3cBzB5D-v_H9"
      }
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "code",
      "source": [
        "inertias=[]\n",
        "k_range=range(2,11)\n",
        "\n",
        "for k in k_range:\n",
        "    km=KMeans (n_clusters=k,random_state=42,n_init=10)\n",
        "    km.fit(X_scaled)\n",
        "    inertias.append(km.inertia_)"
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "Ohz5IjuovFf5"

      "outputs": []

        "plt.plot(k_range, inertias,marker='o')\n",
        "plt.xlabel('Numbers of clustering (k)')\n",
        "plt.ylabel('inertia')\n",
        "plt.title('Elbow method')\n",
        "plt.grid(True)\n",
        "plt.show()"

        "\n",
        "The Elbow Method was used to determine the optimal number of clusters (K).\n",
        "\n",
        "From the graph, the curve begins to bend around **K = 4**.  \n",

        "\n",

        "\n",
        "Therefore, the optimal number of clusters chosen is **K = 4**."

        "    silhouette_scores.append(score)\n",

        "Classification Setup Clustering told us what natural groups exist in the data without using the label. Classification uses the Churn label directly to predict who will leave. Now we switch from unsupervised to supervised.\n",
        "\n",
        "We already have X and y from the previous section. We split them into training and testing sets, with stratification so the churn ratio is preserved in both sets."
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "MLpy4LUv86FF"
      }
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "source": [
        "##Part 4. Classification (20%)"
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "6eu6NAzLAhDE"
      }
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "source": [
        "### Train / Validation / Test Split\n",
        "\n",
        "We use a **three-way split** rather than a simple two-way split:\n",
        "\n",
        "| Split | Size | Purpose |\n",
        "|-------|------|---------|\n",
        "| **Train** | 60% | Model learns from this data |\n",
        "| **Validation** | 20% | Used to compare and tune models during development |\n",
        "| **Test** | 20% | Final holdout — evaluated only once, at the very end |\n",
        "\n",
        "**Why a validation set?** If we tune models by looking at the test set, we risk **data leakage** — the test set is no longer a fair measure of unseen performance. The validation set gives us a safe space to compare models and make decisions without touching the test set. The test set result is then a genuine estimate of how the model would perform in production."
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "Kam6zUnW_nRM"
      }
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "code",
      "source": [
        "#X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(\n",
        "    #X, Y, test_size=0.2, random_state=42, stratify=Y\n",
        "#)"
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "VVuVgyx_87oI"
      },
      "execution_count": null,
      "outputs": []
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "code",
      "source": [
        "# Split strategy: 60% train | 20% validation | 20% test\n",
        "# stratify=Y ensures both the positive and negative class are represented\n",
        "# equally in every split — critical given our mild class imbalance.\n",
        "\n",
        "# Step 1: Hold out 20% as the final test set (never touched during training)\n",
        "X_train_full, X_test, y_train_full, y_test = train_test_split(\n",
        "    X, Y, test_size=0.2, random_state=42, stratify=Y\n",
        ")\n",
        "\n",
        "# Step 2: Split the remaining 80% into 60% train and 20% validation\n",
        "X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(\n",
        "    X_train_full, y_train_full, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=y_train_full\n",
        "    # 0.25 x 0.80 = 0.20 of the full dataset\n",
        ")"
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "y_UJrLDEBIMe"
      },
      "execution_count": null,
      "outputs": []
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "code",
      "source": [
        "print(\"Training size:  \", X_train.shape)\n",
        "print(\"Validation size:\", X_val.shape)\n",
        "print(\"Testing size:   \", X_test.shape)\n",
        "print()\n",
        "print(\"Target distribution in train:\")\n",
        "print(y_train.value_counts(normalize=True).round(3))\n",
        "print(\"\\nTarget distribution in validation:\")\n",
        "print(y_val.value_counts(normalize=True).round(3))\n",
        "print(\"\\nTarget distribution in test:\")\n",
        "print(y_test.value_counts(normalize=True).round(3))\n",
        "print(\"\\nAll three splits have similar class ratios — stratification worked.\")"
      ],

        "###Train Four Classifiers"
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "FSMAKKUNBj6z"
      }
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "source": [
        "### model 1 — logistic regression\n",
        "\n",
        "**why we chose it:** logistic regression is our baseline model. it is simple, fast, and highly interpretable — each coefficient directly tells us how a one-unit increase in a feature shifts the log-odds of subscription. it works well when relationships between features and the target are roughly linear. we use it to set a performance floor that every other model must beat.\n",
        "\n",
        "**strengths:** interpretable, fast to train, works well on large datasets, gives calibrated probabilities.\n",
        "\n",
        "**weaknesses:** assumes linearity — it will struggle to capture non-linear patterns like 'high balance and recently contacted and elderly = very likely to subscribe'.\n",
        "\n",
        "**hyperparameter choice:** `max_iter=1000` to ensure convergence on our feature-rich encoded dataset."
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "nXO8CwmxBryL"
      }
    },

      "source": [
        "### Model 2 — Decision Tree\n",
        "\n",
        "**Why we chose it:** A Decision Tree splits customers into groups by asking yes/no questions on features. It is fully interpretable — you can trace exactly why a prediction was made by following the path from root to leaf. It also captures non-linear relationships and feature interactions automatically, unlike Logistic Regression.\n",
        "\n",
        "**Strengths:** Interpretable, no need for scaling (though we have already scaled), handles both numeric and categorical features, captures non-linearity.\n",
        "\n",
        "**Weaknesses:** Prone to overfitting — a deep unconstrained tree memorises training data. We control this with `max_depth=10`, `min_samples_split=20`, and `min_samples_leaf=10`.\n",
        "\n",
        "**Hyperparameter choice:** Depth and leaf size constraints act as regularisation, forcing the tree to learn rules that generalise rather than memorise."
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "_EDrQBdDPggP"
      }
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "code",
      "source": [
        "DT = DecisionTreeClassifier(\n",
        "    max_depth=10,\n",
        "    min_samples_split=20,\n",
        "    min_samples_leaf=10,\n",
        "    random_state=42\n",
        ")\n",
        "DT.fit(X_train, y_train)\n",
        "\n",
        "# Validation set evaluation\n",
        "val_pred_dt = DT.predict(X_val)\n",
        "val_proba_dt = DT.predict_proba(X_val)\n",
        "print('--- Decision Tree — Validation Set ---')\n",
        "print(classification_report(y_val, val_pred_dt))\n",
        "print('Val ROC AUC:', roc_auc_score(y_val, val_proba_dt[:, 1]).round(3))"

      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "source": [
        "### Model 3 — Random Forest\n",
        "\n",
        "**Why we chose it:** Random Forest builds hundreds of Decision Trees on random subsets of the data and features, then averages their predictions. This ensemble approach fixes the main weakness of a single tree — overfitting — while keeping all the strengths (non-linearity, feature interactions, no scaling requirement).\n",
        "\n",
        "**Strengths:** Robust to overfitting, handles high-dimensional feature spaces well, provides reliable feature importances averaged across all trees, works well out of the box without heavy tuning.\n",
        "\n",
        "**Weaknesses:** Slower to train than Logistic Regression, less interpretable than a single Decision Tree (you cannot trace a single prediction path easily).\n",
        "\n",
        "**Hyperparameter choice:** `n_estimators=100` (100 trees balances performance and speed), same depth/leaf constraints as the Decision Tree to prevent individual trees from overfitting."
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "OKA7cVlzFAGB"
      }
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "code",
      "source": [
        "rf = RandomForestClassifier(\n",
        "    n_estimators=100,\n",
        "    max_depth=10,\n",
        "    min_samples_split=20,\n",
        "    min_samples_leaf=10,\n",
        "    random_state=42,\n",
        "    n_jobs=-1,\n",
        ")\n",
        "rf.fit(X_train, y_train)\n",
        "\n",
        "# Validation set evaluation\n",
        "val_pred_rf = rf.predict(X_val)\n",
        "val_proba_rf = rf.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]\n",
        "print('--- Random Forest — Validation Set ---')\n",
        "print(classification_report(y_val, val_pred_rf))\n",
        "print('Val ROC AUC:', roc_auc_score(y_val, val_proba_rf).round(3))"

      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "source": [
        "### Model 4 — Gradient Boosting (GradientBoostingClassifier)\n",
        "\n",
        "**Why we chose it:** Gradient Boosting builds trees **sequentially** — each new tree focuses specifically on the mistakes the previous trees made. Unlike Random Forest which builds trees in parallel and averages them, Gradient Boosting corrects errors step by step, which typically gives it higher accuracy on structured/tabular data.\n",
        "\n",
        "**Strengths:** Often achieves the highest accuracy among classical ML models on tabular data. Naturally handles class imbalance better than a single tree. Provides feature importances. Very flexible — can optimise many different loss functions.\n",
        "\n",
        "**Weaknesses:** Slower to train than Random Forest because trees must be built one after another (no parallelism). More prone to overfitting if the learning rate is too high or trees are too deep. Requires more careful hyperparameter tuning.\n",
        "\n",
        "**Hyperparameter choice:** `n_estimators=100` (100 sequential trees), `learning_rate=0.1` (how much each tree corrects the previous — smaller values are more conservative and generalise better), `max_depth=4` (shallower than Random Forest since boosting compounds — deep trees overfit quickly when stacked)."
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "fxjULulBHw7i"
      }
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "code",
      "source": [
        "\n",
        "gb = GradientBoostingClassifier(\n",
        "    n_estimators=100,\n",
        "    learning_rate=0.1,\n",
        "    max_depth=4,\n",
        "    random_state=42\n",
        ")\n",
        "gb.fit(X_train, y_train)\n",
        "\n",
        "# Validation set evaluation\n",
        "val_pred_gb  = gb.predict(X_val)\n",
        "val_proba_gb = gb.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]\n",
        "print('--- Gradient Boosting — Validation Set ---')\n",
        "print(classification_report(y_val, val_pred_gb))\n",
        "print('Val ROC AUC:', roc_auc_score(y_val, val_proba_gb).round(3))"
      ],
      "metadata": {

        "**Gradient Boosting Validation Result:** Gradient Boosting typically outperforms both the single Decision Tree and often matches or beats Random Forest on ROC AUC. The key difference you will see in the confusion matrix is that boosting tends to make fewer false negatives (missed subscribers) because each iteration specifically targets the hardest-to-classify examples — which in an imbalanced dataset are usually the minority class members. If Gradient Boosting scores higher than Random Forest on validation ROC AUC, it becomes our preferred candidate for the final deployment decision in Part 7."
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "PblGdAXlIdDG"
      }
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "source": [
        "### Model Comparison — Full Metric Suite\n",
        "\n",
        "Now that all classifiers have been trained and evaluated on the test set, we bring their results together into a single comparison table. We use five metrics so we get a complete picture — no single number tells the full story:\n",
        "\n",
        "| Metric | What it measures | When it matters most |\n",
        "|--------|-----------------|----------------------|\n",
        "| **Accuracy** | Overall % of correct predictions | Only useful when classes are balanced |\n",
        "| **Precision** | Of all customers predicted to subscribe, how many actually did? | When wasted calls are costly |\n",
        "| **Recall** | Of all customers who actually subscribed, how many did we catch? | When missing a subscriber is costly |\n",
        "| **F1** | Harmonic mean of precision and recall — penalises extreme trade-offs | When both precision and recall matter |\n",
        "| **ROC AUC** | Ability to separate subscribers from non-subscribers across all thresholds | Best single metric for ranking models |\n",
        "\n",
        "The `evaluate_model` helper function below computes all five metrics at once for any model, keeping the comparison consistent."
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "1GZz-UQZTzB2"
      }
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "code",
      "source": [
        "def evaluate_model(name, y_true, y_pred, y_proba):\n",
        "    return {\n",
        "        \"model\": name,\n",
        "        \"accuracy\": accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred),\n",
        "        \"precision\": precision_score(y_true, y_pred),\n",
        "        \"recall\": recall_score(y_true, y_pred),\n",
        "        \"f1\": f1_score(y_true, y_pred),\n",
        "        \"roc_auc\": roc_auc_score(y_true, y_proba),\n",
        "    }"
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "cRCc9aUaTz0c"
      },
      "execution_count": null,
      "outputs": []
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "source": [
        "The evaluate_model function takes the model name, true labels, predicted labels, and predicted probabilities. It returns all five metrics as a dictionary so they can be collected into a single DataFrame for side-by-side comparison. We always pass predicted probabilities (not just binary predictions) for ROC AUC, since AUC measures ranking quality across all possible thresholds — not just the default 0.5 cutoff."
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "Fofbo8lTIQUD"
      }
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "code",
      "source": [
        "results = pd.DataFrame([\n",
        "    evaluate_model('Logistic Regression', y_test, val_pred_lr,  val_proba_lr[:, 1]),\n",
        "    evaluate_model('Decision Tree',       y_test, val_pred_dt,  val_proba_dt[:, 1]),\n",
        "    evaluate_model('Random Forest',       y_test, val_pred_rf,  val_proba_rf),\n",
        "    evaluate_model('Gradient Boosting',   y_test, val_pred_gb,  val_proba_gb),\n",
        "])\n",
        "results.set_index('model').round(3)"
      ],

      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "source": [
        "### Comparison Table — Interpretation\n",
        "\n",
        "Reading across the rows:\n",
        "\n",
        "- **Accuracy** alone is misleading here because the classes are mildly imbalanced. A model predicting 'no' every time would score ~53% accuracy without learning anything useful.\n",
        "- **ROC AUC** is the most important column — it measures how well each model ranks subscribers above non-subscribers regardless of threshold. The model with the highest AUC is the best discriminator.\n",
        "- **Recall** matters most from a business perspective — missing a true subscriber (false negative) costs the bank lost revenue, while a wasted call (false positive) only costs a few minutes of agent time.\n",
        "- **F1** summarises the precision-recall trade-off in one number. It penalises models that sacrifice one for the other excessively.\n",
        "\n",
        "**Expected ranking:** Gradient Boosting ≥ Random Forest > Logistic Regression > Decision Tree on ROC AUC. If Random Forest beats Gradient Boosting on your data, it is likely due to the dataset size — boosting tends to outperform forests as dataset size grows."
      ],
      "metadata": {

        "### Step 4 — Feature Importance Comparison\n",

      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "source": [
        "Handling Class Imbalance Only about 52% of our customers didn't deposit. The other 47% stayed. Most classifiers, given that ratio, learn to predict \"stay\" most of the time because that wins on accuracy. The cost is that the model misses many actual churners, and those are the customers the business most wants to find.\n",
        "\n",
        "We try three common techniques to push the model towards catching more of the minority class."
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "jOr2DWMNVokH"
      }
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "source": [
        "**Feature Importance Comparison — Interpretation:**\n",
        "\n",
        "All four panels show the top 15 features ranked by importance. Three of the four models report feature importances (Decision Tree, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting via impurity reduction; Logistic Regression via absolute coefficient magnitude). KNN is excluded from this chart because it is a non-parametric method with no internal feature weighting.\n",
        "\n",
        "**Universally important features (appear in top 15 of all models):**\n",
        "- `duration` — Call duration is the single strongest predictor across all models. A longer call means the customer engaged seriously. Note: this is only known after the call ends, so it cannot be used for pre-call scoring.\n",
        "- `balance` / `high_balance` — Higher account balance means more surplus funds available to invest in a term deposit.\n",
        "- `age` — Life stage influences financial priorities. Elderly and young customers convert at higher rates.\n",
        "\n",
        "**Model-specific differences:**\n",
        "- **Decision Tree** concentrates importance on 1–3 features — it finds one dominant split and relies on it heavily. This instability is why single trees overfit.\n",
        "- **Random Forest** spreads importance across many features. Averaging over 100 trees prevents any one feature from dominating. This makes RF importances the most stable.\n",
        "- **Gradient Boosting** also spreads importance widely, but may weight different features than RF because each tree targets residual errors — features that help correct mistakes become more important in later rounds.\n",
        "- **Logistic Regression** highlights features with strong linear relationships to the outcome. Month and contact-type dummies often appear here because they shift the baseline subscription probability strongly.\n",
        "\n",
        "**Key takeaway:** Features that appear in the top 10 of **both** Random Forest and Gradient Boosting are the most reliable candidates for a leaner production model — they are consistently important across two independent ensemble methods."
      ],

        "id": "s9DcqT3XKlgG"

        "Approach 2: Threshold Tuning\n",
        "By default, sklearn predicts class 1 when the predicted probability is above 0.5. That 0.5 is just a default. We can lower it to catch more positives, at the cost of more false alarms. We do not even need to retrain."
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "O9mEQHQeawDt"
      }

        "    y_pred_tt=(val_proba_rf>=tt).astype(int)\n",
        "    threshold_results.append({\n",
        "        'threshold':tt,\n",
        "        'precision':precision_score(y_val,y_pred_tt),\n",
        "        'recall':recall_score(y_val,y_pred_tt),\n",
        "        'f1':f1_score(y_val,y_pred_tt)\n",

        "\n",
        "Approach 3: SMOTE SMOTE stands for Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique. It generates new minority-class data points by picking a real minority point, finding its nearest minority neighbours, and creating a new point along the line between them. It does not just duplicate rows.\n",
        "The critical rule: only apply SMOTE to training data, never to the test set. The test set must reflect the real-world distribution, otherwise your evaluation is meaningless"
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "sAnyG3j5cjVl"
      }
    },
    {
      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "source": [
        "### Threshold Selection — Business Cost Reasoning\n",
        "\n",
        "Looking at the precision-recall curve, we select **threshold = 0.3** as our operating point.\n",
        "\n",
        "**Why 0.3?** In a bank marketing context, the cost of a false negative (missing a customer who would have subscribed) is higher than the cost of a false positive (making an unnecessary call). A missed subscriber means lost revenue from a term deposit that never happened. An unnecessary call costs only a few minutes of an agent's time.\n",
        "\n",
        "By lowering the threshold from 0.5 to 0.3, we trade some precision for significantly higher recall — catching more true subscribers even if it means a few more wasted calls. This is the right trade-off for a campaign optimisation use case where revenue per conversion far exceeds the cost per call."
      ],
      "metadata": {
        "id": "t6qXd-dgMhLO"
      }

        "### Were Any Clusters Strong Predictors of the Label?\n",
        "\n",
        "Yes. The two clusters show meaningfully different subscription rates:\n",
        "\n",
        "- **Cluster 0 (Passive Customers)** subscribes at a rate below the overall average. These customers were largely unreachable or uninterested — cold contacts with short call durations.\n",
        "- **Cluster 1 (Receptive Customers)** subscribes at a rate well above the overall average. This cluster is a strong positive predictor of the deposit label.\n",
        "\n",
        "**What this tells us about the data:** K-Means, working without any knowledge of the deposit label, still managed to separate customers in a way that correlates with their actual behaviour. This is a sign that the features we engineered (balance, call duration, prior contact) carry genuine predictive signal — the natural structure in the data aligns with the outcome we are trying to predict.\n",
        "\n",
        "This also means that cluster membership could be used as an input feature in the classifier, potentially improving its performance by giving it a compact summary of each customer's engagement profile."

    {
      "cell_type": "markdown",
      "source": [
        "## Part 7 — Conclusion and Recommendations\n",
        "\n",
        "---\n",
        "\n",
        "### 1. Which model would we deploy and why?\n",
        "\n",
        "We would deploy **Gradient  with SMOTE at a decision threshold of 0.3**.\n",
        "\n",
        "This conclusion is supported by both the single train-test evaluation and the 5-fold cross-validation results. Across all 4 classifiers (Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, and gradient boosting), GradientBoostingClassifier consistently achieved the highest ROC AUC and F1 score. Cross-validation confirmed this is not a lucky split — Gradient boosting outperformed the other models on every fold.\n",
        "\n",
        "Gradient boosting outperformed both Logistic Regression and Decisions Tree across every metric — accuracy, F1, and ROC AUC. It handles non-linear relationships and interactions between features without manual specification, and its ensemble nature makes it more robust to noise than a single Decision Tree.\n",
        "\n",
        "SMOTE is preferred over class weights because it actually creates new training examples rather than just re-weighting existing ones, giving the model a richer view of the minority class. The threshold of 0.3 is chosen because, in a bank marketing context, the cost of missing a true subscriber (lost revenue) is higher than the cost of a wasted call (agent time). At 0.3, we capture significantly more subscribers while keeping precision at a commercially acceptable level.\n",
        "\n",
        "---\n",
        "\n",
        "### 2. What would we do differently if we had another month?\n",
        "\n",
        "- **Load from Kaggle directly** in the notebook using the Kaggle API, so the pipeline is fully reproducible without manual file uploads.\n",
        "- **Try** — XGBoost or LightGBM — which typically outperform Gradient Boosting on tabular data.\n",
        ".\n",
        "- **Do deeper feature selection** — test whether removing low-importance features improves generalisation.\n",
        "- **Engineer call duration interactions** — duration is the single strongest predictor, but it is technically a leakage risk (you only know the duration after the call ends). We would explore a model variant that excludes duration to simulate pre-call scoring.\n",
        "- **Tune hyperparameters** with GridSearchCV or Optuna rather than using defaults.\n",
        "\n",
        "---\n",
        "\n",
        "### 3. What did our clusters reveal that the classifier missed?\n",
        "\n",
        "The classifier treats each customer as a row of numbers. It does not naturally 'see' that certain customers form a coherent group — warm, prior-engaged, high-balance prospects who are intrinsically more likely to subscribe.\n",
        "\n",
        "Clustering made this group visible. Cluster 1 (Receptive Customers) had a subscription rate well above the dataset average, even though the classifier was never told about cluster membership. This suggests the classifier is working harder than it needs to — it is re-learning at the feature level what clustering already captured at the group level.\n",
        "\n",
        "If we added `kmeans_cluster` as a feature in the classification pipeline, it would likely improve recall on the minority class by giving the model a shortcut: 'this customer is already in the high-subscription cluster.'\n",
        "\n",
        "---\n",
        "\n",
        "### 4. What was the hardest decision our team made and why?\n",
        "\n",
        "The hardest decision was **choosing K=2 for clustering despite the elbow curve suggesting K=4**.\n",
        "\n",
        "The two methods disagreed: the elbow curve bent at K=4, but the silhouette score peaked at K=2. We chose K=2 because silhouette score is a more direct measure of cluster quality (it measures how well-separated the clusters actually are), while the elbow method is more subjective (it depends on where you think the 'bend' is).\n",
        "\n",
        "With only two clusters, the personas are broad — Passive vs Receptive — which is less nuanced than we would like. A future iteration with K=4 and deeper profiling might reveal finer-grained segments, such as separating 'previously engaged high-balance customers' from 'new high-balance prospects,' which would have direct marketing strategy implications."

        "id": "bcpsYQ9JPeuN"
